Interesting read but I dont think that the success rates are very high with these tools. For several years now WIFI routers are shipped with WPA2 and secure (un-guessable) default passwords. It should also be obvious that brute force attackes are recognized by firewalls and if you really manages to connect to a router your device will be logged. Inside the lan, your system is open to any other device connected and finally zeroconf services will unmask you in a matter of seconds.
When it comes down to it with WPA2, you are better off looking around for a sticky note with the password on it...
I've used some of the techniques outlined in the article to try to hack my neighbors wifi just to see if it would work and I can also say that I think the stick note route is a better one.

Yeah I mean you can get a handshake fairly easily if you know what you are doing - so you can at least attempt the brute force without having to actually be within distance of the router - but brute forcing requires either time, knowledge of likely hits, or massive resources. Usually a combo of the three is what it takes.

Why? most home ones have a quick connect button that you can press and connect instead of using the password, so if you have access to the desk just use that or look at the sticker on the combo modem.

I didn't specifically mean the sticky note, I just meant that WPA-2 is not possible to hack without brute force, so unless you can guess the passcode there's little use in trying. So you're better off just having the password or giving up.

The 'quick connect' you describe is actually a quite good way in for a hacker, even without physical access to the router. Quite a few implementations of WPS are dodgy as fuck. I always advise to turn that shit off.
